hs_math_t04_st01.title: Linear equations in one variable
hs_math_t04_st01.overview: A linear equation in one variable states that two expressions have the same value. Solving it means finding the value of the variable that makes the equality true. The key principle is to preserve equality by performing the same valid operation on both sides.

key_concepts.definition: Maintain balance on both sides.
details: An equation such as $x+5=12$ states that its left-hand and right-hand sides have equal values.
To isolate the variable, use inverse operations and apply each operation to both sides. For example, subtract $5$ from both sides to obtain $x=7$.

key_concepts.definition: A simplified linear equation.
details: After collecting all variable terms on one side and constants on the other, a linear equation in one variable can be written as $ax+b=0$.
When $a\ne0$, the equation has the unique solution $x=-\frac{b}{a}$. If simplification gives $0=b$ with $b\ne0$, there is no solution; if it gives $0=0$, every permitted real value is a solution.

key_concepts.definition: Substitute the value into the original equation.
details: A value is a solution only if it makes the original left-hand and right-hand sides equal.
Substitution is an effective way to check the result and can reveal sign or arithmetic errors.

common_mistakes.mistake: Performing an operation on only one side of an equation.
common_mistakes.correction: To preserve equality, apply the same operation to both sides. For example, subtracting $5$ on the left requires subtracting $5$ on the right.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating every simplified equation as having one solution.
common_mistakes.correction: After simplifying, check the resulting statement. A false constant equality means no solution; a true identity means infinitely many solutions.

hs_math_t04_st02.title: Linear equations in two variables
hs_math_t04_st02.overview: A linear equation in two variables describes all ordered pairs that make the equation true. When the coefficients are real and the equation represents a non-degenerate linear relation, its graph is a straight line. Each point on that line is a solution pair.

key_concepts.definition: A pair that satisfies the equation.
details: A solution is written as $(x,y)$. For $x+y=10$, the pair $(2,8)$ is a solution because $2+8=10$.
One linear equation in two variables generally has infinitely many real solution pairs, which form a straight line when plotted.

key_concepts.definition: The form that shows gradient and vertical intercept.
details: For a non-vertical line, the equation can be written as $y=mx+c$.
The slope or gradient $m$ measures vertical change divided by horizontal change. The $y$-intercept is the point $(0,c)$.
A vertical line has equation $x=k$ and an undefined slope, so it cannot be written as $y=mx+c$.

key_concepts.definition: Reading key features from an equation or two points.
details: Find the $y$-intercept by setting $x=0$, and find the $x$-intercept by setting $y=0$, when those intercepts exist.
For two points with different $x$-coordinates, the slope is the change in $y$ divided by the change in $x$.

solution_steps: Step 1: Isolate $y$: subtract $3x$ from both sides to obtain $y=-3x+9$.
Step 3: The slope is $m=-3$, and the $y$-intercept is $(0,9)$.

common_mistakes.correction: In $y=mx+c$, the coefficient of $x$ is the slope, while the constant $c$ gives the $y$-intercept $(0,c)$.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the slope formula when the two $x$-coordinates are equal.
common_mistakes.correction: If $x_2=x_1$, the line is vertical and its slope is undefined.

A non-vertical straight line can be written as $y=mx+c$.
Slope is rise divided by run; the $y$-intercept is $(0,c)$.
Vertical lines have undefined slope.

hs_math_t04_st03.title: Simultaneous linear equations
hs_math_t04_st03.overview: A system of simultaneous linear equations is a collection of two or more linear equations considered together. A solution to a two-equation system is an ordered pair that satisfies both equations at the same time, not just one of them.

key_concepts.definition: Equations considered together.
details: A system may contain two linear equations in the same two variables, such as $2x+y=7$ and $x-y=2$.
The equations impose conditions on the same unknown values, so their solutions must satisfy every equation in the system.

key_concepts.definition: One pair that satisfies every equation.
details: For a system in $x$ and $y$, a solution is an ordered pair $(x,y)$ that makes each equation true when substituted.
A pair that satisfies only one equation is not a solution of the system.

key_concepts.definition: One, none or infinitely many.
details: Two non-parallel distinct lines meet at one point, giving one solution.
Parallel distinct lines have no common point, so the system has no solution.
Coincident lines are the same line, so every point on that line is a common solution and the system has infinitely many solutions. The graphical interpretation is developed in the next lesson.

worked_examples.problem: Check whether $(3,1)$ is a solution of the system $2x+y=7$ and $x-y=2$.
solution_steps: Step 1: Substitute $x=3$, $y=1$ into the first equation: $2(3)+1=7$. This is true.
Step 2: Substitute into the second equation: $3-1=2$. This is also true.
Step 3: The pair satisfies both equations, so it is a common solution.
worked_examples.final_answer: Yes, $(3,1)$ is a solution of the system.

worked_examples.problem: Check whether $(2,3)$ is a solution of $x+y=5$ and $2x-y=1$.
solution_steps: Step 1: First equation: $2+3=5$, which is true.
Step 2: Second equation: $2(2)-3=1$, which is true.
worked_examples.final_answer: Yes, $(2,3)$ is a solution of the system.

common_mistakes.mistake: Checking a proposed pair in only one equation.
common_mistakes.correction: Substitute the pair into every equation. It is a solution of the system only if all equations are satisfied.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming every system has exactly one solution.
common_mistakes.correction: A system of two linear equations may have one solution, no solution or infinitely many solutions.

quick_summary: A simultaneous system is a group of equations in the same variables.
A solution pair must satisfy every equation in the system.
A system of two linear equations may have one, no or infinitely many solutions.
Graphical and algebraic ways to determine the solutions are covered in the next lessons.

hs_math_t04_st04.title: Graphical solutions of simultaneous equations
hs_math_t04_st04.overview: A graphical solution of a simultaneous linear system is the point where the graphs of the equations meet. Plot both lines on the same coordinate plane, then identify any common point. The number and position of intersections show how many solutions the system has.

key_concepts.definition: Draw both lines on the same axes.
details: Rewrite each equation in a form that makes plotting convenient, or find at least two points on each line.
Use the same coordinate scale for both equations and draw both straight lines on the same set of axes.
The intersection coordinate is the graphical solution of the system.

key_concepts.definition: One, none or infinitely many solutions.
details: If the lines cross at one point, there is one solution.
If the lines are parallel and distinct, they never meet and there is no solution.
If the lines coincide, every point on the line is shared and there are infinitely many solutions.

key_concepts.definition: Read coordinates with care.
details: A graph drawn on paper may give an approximate intersection, especially when the coordinates are not integers.
Use substitution or elimination when an exact solution is required. The algebraic methods are taught in the next subtopic.

worked_examples.problem: Find the graphical solution of $y=2x+1$ and $y=-x+7$.
solution_steps: Step 1: For $y=2x+1$, plot points such as $(0,1)$ and $(2,5)$.
Step 2: For $y=-x+7$, plot points such as $(0,7)$ and $(2,5)$.
Step 3: Draw both straight lines. They meet at $(2,5)$.
Step 4: The common point is the solution because it lies on both lines.

worked_examples.problem: Describe the number of solutions when the graphs of two equations are parallel and distinct.
solution_steps: Step 1: Parallel distinct lines have the same direction but different positions.
Step 2: They do not intersect at any point.
Step 3: Therefore, no ordered pair satisfies both equations.

common_mistakes.mistake: Plotting the two equations on different coordinate scales.
common_mistakes.correction: Use the same axes and scale for both graphs so the intersection can be identified correctly.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating a visually estimated coordinate as exact.
common_mistakes.correction: A graph may provide only an approximation. Verify the exact point algebraically when exact values are needed.

The intersection point is a common solution pair.

hs_math_t04_st05.title: Substitution and elimination methods
hs_math_t04_st05.overview: Substitution and elimination are algebraic methods for finding the exact common solution of a system of two linear equations. Choose a method that keeps the arithmetic manageable, then check the resulting ordered pair in both original equations.

key_concepts.definition: Express one variable and replace it.
details: Rearrange one equation to make a variable the subject, such as $y=12-x$.
Substitute that complete expression into the other equation. Solve the resulting equation in one variable, then substitute back to find the second variable.

key_concepts.definition: Combine equations to remove a variable.
details: Write the equations in aligned form.
Multiply one or both equations by suitable non-zero constants so that the coefficients of one variable are equal or opposites.
Add or subtract the equations to eliminate that variable, solve for the remaining variable, and substitute back.

key_concepts.definition: Recognising inconsistent and dependent systems.
details: If elimination produces a false statement such as $0=3$, the system has no solution.
If elimination produces a true statement such as $0=0$, the equations represent the same line and the system has infinitely many solutions.

worked_examples.problem: Solve using substitution: $x + y = 12$ and $2x - y = 3$.
solution_steps: Step 1: Make $y$ the subject of the first equation: $y = 12 - x$.
Step 2: Substitute this entire block into the second equation: $2x - (12 - x) = 3$.
Step 3: Distribute the negative sign: $2x - 12 + x = 3$.
Step 5: Plug $x=5$ back into $y = 12 - x$ to get $y = 12 - 5 = 7$.
Step 1: Neither variable matches. Multiply the top by $3$ and the bottom by $2$ to force the $x$ coefficients to match at $6$.
Step 3: Subtract the bottom from the top: $(6x - 6x) + (9y - 4y) = 39 - 24 \implies 5y = 15 \implies y = 3$.
Step 4: Plug $y=3$ into the original first equation: $2x + 3(3) = 13 \implies 2x + 9 = 13 \implies 2x = 4 \implies x = 2$.

common_mistakes.correction: When multiplying an equation by a constant, multiply every term on both sides, including the constant term.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stopping after finding the first variable.
common_mistakes.correction: Substitute back to find the second variable, then check the ordered pair in both original equations.

quick_summary: Substitution replaces one variable with an equivalent expression.
Elimination combines equations to remove one variable.
A false constant statement means no solution; a true identity means infinitely many solutions.
Check the final pair in both original equations.

hs_math_t04_st06.title: Quadratic equations by factorisation
hs_math_t04_st06.overview: A quadratic equation has degree 2. Its solutions are the values of the variable that make the equation true. When the corresponding quadratic function is graphed, these solutions are the x-coordinates where its graph intersects the x-axis.

key_concepts.definition: The standard equation form
details: Before factorising a quadratic equation, rearrange it so that one side is zero: $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$, where $a\ne0$.

key_concepts.definition: A property used to solve a product equation
details: If the product of two real numbers or expressions is zero, at least one factor must be zero: $AB=0$ implies $A=0$ or $B=0$.

key_concepts.definition: Solving each factor equation
details: After factorising, set each factor equal to zero and solve the resulting linear equations.
For example, if a factor is $(x-5)$, its zero is $x=5$.

solution_steps: Step 1: Check standard form. It already equals zero.
Step 2: Factorise. Find numbers that multiply to $12$ and add to $7$. The numbers are $3$ and $4$.
Step 4: Apply the zero-product property. $x + 3 = 0 \implies x = -3$. $x + 4 = 0 \implies x = -4$.
Step 1: Rearrange into standard form: Subtract $8x$ to set it to zero: $2x^2 - 8x = 0$.
Step 2: Factorise out the common factor of $2x$: $2x(x - 4) = 0$.
Step 3: Apply the zero-product property. Either $2x = 0 \implies x = 0$, or $x - 4 = 0 \implies x = 4$.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dividing both sides by a variable.
common_mistakes.correction: Dividing by a variable can remove a valid solution. For example, dividing $2x^2=8x$ by $x$ assumes $x\ne0$ and loses the solution $x=0$. Instead, rearrange and factorise: $2x(x-4)=0$, so $x=0$ or $x=4$.

common_mistakes.mistake: Applying Zero-Product to a number other than zero.
common_mistakes.correction: The zero-product property applies only when a product equals zero. If $(x-2)(x-3)=12$, first expand and rearrange the equation to make one side zero; do not set either factor equal to 12.

hs_math_t04_st07.title: Completing the square
hs_math_t04_st07.overview: Completing the square rewrites a quadratic expression as a squared binomial plus or minus a constant. This makes it possible to solve quadratic equations that do not factorise neatly and reveals the vertex form of a quadratic graph.

key_concepts.concept: Completing the Square for a Monic Quadratic
key_concepts.definition: Create a perfect-square trinomial.
details: For $x^2+bx=c$, take half the coefficient of $x$, square that value, and add it to both sides.
The left side becomes $(x+\frac{b}{2})^2$, which can then be solved using square roots.

key_concepts.concept: When the Leading Coefficient Is Not One
key_concepts.definition: Make the coefficient of x squared equal to one first.
details: For $ax^2+bx+c=0$ with $a\ne0$, divide through by $a$ before completing the square.
After dividing, halve the coefficient of $x$ and square it. Add this value to both sides to form a perfect square.

key_concepts.definition: Read the turning point of a quadratic graph.
details: A quadratic written as $y=a(x-h)^2+k$ has vertex $(h,k)$.
When $a>0$ the graph opens upward and the vertex is a minimum; when $a<0$ it opens downward and the vertex is a maximum.

hs_math_t04_st08.title: Quadratic formula
hs_math_t04_st08.overview: The quadratic formula gives the solutions of any quadratic equation with real coefficients, provided the equation is written in standard form and the leading coefficient is non-zero. It is especially useful when factorisation is difficult or does not produce simple rational roots.

key_concepts.definition: Substitute the coefficients from standard form.
details: First write the equation as $ax^2+bx+c=0$, with $a\ne0$.
Identify the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$, including their signs, then substitute them into the formula.

key_concepts.definition: Evaluate both branches.
details: The symbol $\pm$ means calculate once using addition and once using subtraction.
The two values may be distinct or equal, depending on the discriminant.

key_concepts.definition: Keep surds exact unless an estimate is required.
details: An exact answer retains a simplified radical, such as $\frac{3\pm\sqrt5}{2}$.
An approximate answer is a decimal rounded to a stated number of places. Keep the exact form during working to avoid rounding error.

hs_math_t04_st09.title: Nature of roots and discriminant
hs_math_t04_st09.overview: The discriminant is the part of the quadratic formula under the square root. Its sign determines whether a quadratic equation has two distinct real roots, one repeated real root or no real roots.

key_concepts.definition: A quantity that classifies the roots.
details: For $ax^2+bx+c=0$, the discriminant is $\Delta=b^2-4ac$.
It is the expression under the square root in the quadratic formula.

key_concepts.definition: Interpret the sign of the discriminant.
details: If $\Delta>0$, there are two distinct real roots and the parabola crosses the $x$-axis twice.
If $\Delta=0$, there is one repeated real root and the parabola touches the $x$-axis at its vertex.
If $\Delta<0$, there are no real roots. For real coefficients, the equation has two non-real complex conjugate roots.

key_concepts.definition: Use the coefficient assumptions.
details: When $a$, $b$ and $c$ are rational and $\Delta>0$, a perfect-square rational discriminant gives rational roots.
When $a$, $b$ and $c$ are rational and $\Delta>0$ is not a perfect square rational number, the roots are irrational.
The sign of the discriminant alone determines the number of real roots; whether the roots are rational also depends on the coefficients.

hs_math_t04_st10.title: Linear inequalities
hs_math_t04_st10.overview: Inequalities describe a world of possibilities rather than a single fixed answer. Solving them works almost exactly like solving equations, with one crucial, rule-breaking exception involving negative numbers.

key_concepts.definition: The big exception.
details: When you multiply or divide BOTH sides of an inequality by a **NEGATIVE** number, the inequality sign MUST flip to face the other direction.
Example: $-2x > 8 \implies x < -4$.

key_concepts.definition: Drawing the boundary.
details: **Open Circle ($\circ$):** Used for $<$ and $>$. The boundary number is excluded.
**Closed Circle ($\bullet$):** Used for $\le$ and $\ge$. The boundary number is included.
The arrow points in the direction of the solution.

key_concepts.definition: The shorthand bracket code.
details: **Parentheses ( ):** Endpoint is excluded (matches open circle). ALWAYS used for Infinity ($\infty$ or $-\infty$).
**Square Brackets [ ]:** Endpoint is included (matches closed circle).

hs_math_t04_st11.title: Compound inequalities
hs_math_t04_st11.overview: Compound inequalities combine two separate conditions into a single mathematical sentence using the words 'AND' or 'OR'. They are used to define bounded ranges or completely separate, diverging intervals.

key_concepts.definition: The 'Sandwich'.
details: Both conditions MUST be true at the same time.
Usually written as a double inequality, bounding the variable between a floor and a ceiling: $-3 < x \le 5$.
On a number line, this looks like a continuous line segment drawn between two endpoints.

key_concepts.definition: The 'Split'.
details: Only ONE of the conditions needs to be true.
Usually written as two separate inequalities: $x < 2 \text{ OR } x > 7$.
On a number line, this looks like two arrows shooting in opposite directions, leaving an empty gap in the middle. Interval notation uses the Union symbol $\cup$.

key_concepts.definition: The three-part balance.
details: To solve an expression like $1 < x + 4 < 10$, whatever you do to the middle, you must do to the LEFT and the RIGHT. Subtract $4$ from all three zones: $-3 < x < 6$.

hs_math_t04_st12.title: Quadratic inequalities
hs_math_t04_st12.overview: Solving quadratic inequalities requires finding the roots of the parabola and then determining which sections of the curve dip below the x-axis (negative) or rise above it (positive).

key_concepts.definition: Locate the real roots of the quadratic.
details: Move all terms to one side and find the real roots of the associated quadratic equation.
The roots divide the number line into intervals on which the quadratic expression keeps a constant sign, provided the polynomial is not identically zero.

key_concepts.definition: Test the sign in each interval.
details: Choose one test value from each interval and substitute it into the factored expression, or use the signs of its factors.
Select the intervals where the expression is positive or negative as required by the inequality.

key_concepts.definition: Read the inequality sign.
details: For a strict inequality ($< $ or $>$), roots where the expression equals zero are excluded.
For a non-strict inequality ($\le$ or $\ge$), include any real roots that satisfy the original inequality.

key_concepts.definition: Use the position of the parabola relative to the x-axis.
details: For an upward-opening parabola with two distinct roots, the quadratic is negative between the roots and positive outside them.
For a downward-opening parabola, the sign pattern is reversed. Sign analysis works in both cases and is safer than memorising only the upward-opening pattern.

  <text x="270" y="104" text-anchor="middle" fill="#166534" font-size="18" font-weight="bold">−</text>

solution_steps: Step 2: The critical points are $1$ and $5$.
Step 3: Test the intervals. At $x=0$, the product is positive; at $x=2$, it is negative; at $x=6$, it is positive.
Step 4: Choose the interval where the expression is negative. Because the inequality is strict, exclude both roots.
Step 3: Divide by $-4$ and reverse the inequality: $t(t-4)\le0$.
Step 4: The product is non-positive between the roots, including the endpoints.

common_mistakes.mistake: Solving it like a linear inequality.
common_mistakes.correction: If you have $x^2 > 9$, you CANNOT just take the square root and say $x > 3$. You are completely missing the negative root! $x^2 - 9 > 0 \implies (x-3)(x+3) > 0$. The correct answer is $x > 3$ OR $x < -3$.

quick_summary: Find the critical points by factoring.
Use a number line test or visualize the parabola.
$> 0$ usually means OR (outside the roots).
$< 0$ usually means AND (between the roots).

hs_math_t04_st13.title: Equations involving rational expressions
hs_math_t04_st13.overview: A rational equation contains one or more algebraic fractions in which the variable may appear in a denominator. Solve by identifying forbidden denominator values, clearing fractions with a common denominator, and checking every candidate in the original equation.

key_concepts.definition: Values that make an original denominator zero are excluded.
details: Before solving, set each original denominator equal to zero and record the values that are not allowed.
These restrictions remain in force even if a factor cancels during simplification.

key_concepts.definition: Multiply every term by the least common denominator.
details: Find the least common denominator of all rational terms.
Multiply every term on both sides by that denominator, making sure no term is omitted. Solve the resulting polynomial equation.

key_concepts.definition: Reject candidates outside the original domain.
details: Clearing denominators may produce candidate values that make an original denominator zero.
Substitute each candidate into the original equation. Reject any value that makes the original expression undefined or does not satisfy the equation.

solution_steps: Step 2: The least common denominator is $x(x+1)$. Multiply every term by it: $2(x+1)+3x=2x(x+1)$.
Step 5: Neither candidate is excluded by the original restrictions, so both are valid.
Step 2: A fraction is zero when its numerator is zero and its denominator is non-zero. Solve $x^2-4=0$.
Step 4: Reject $x=2$ because it makes the original denominator zero. The value $x=-2$ is valid.

common_mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to multiply the constant term by the LCD.
common_mistakes.correction: When clearing fractions in $\frac{x}{3} = \frac{2}{x} + 4$, you must multiply the $4$ by the LCD as well! It becomes $x^2 = 6 + 12x$, NOT $x^2 = 6 + 4$.

common_mistakes.mistake: Accepting all answers blindly.
common_mistakes.correction: You MUST check your final roots against the original denominators. If an answer makes any original denominator zero, you must cross it out.

quick_summary: Find domain restrictions immediately.
Multiply every term by the LCD to destroy all fractions.
Solve the resulting linear or quadratic equation.
Reject any extraneous solutions.

hs_math_t04_st14.title: Equations involving radicals
hs_math_t04_st14.overview: Radical equations feature variables trapped inside square roots, cube roots, or higher powers. To free the variable, we must isolate the radical and raise both sides of the equation to the matching power.

key_concepts.definition: Clear the area.
details: Before you square both sides, the square root must be completely alone on one side of the equals sign.
If you have $\sqrt{x} + 3 = 8$, you MUST subtract $3$ first to get $\sqrt{x} = 5$ before squaring.

key_concepts.definition: Creating fake answers.
details: Squaring both sides of an equation is not a perfectly reversible operation (e.g., $(-3)^2 = 9$ and $3^2 = 9$).
Because of this, squaring both sides can create **extraneous solutions** that work in the squared version but fail in the original equation. You MUST plug answers back in to check.

key_concepts.definition: No negative insides.
details: For a real square root (or 4th root, 6th root), the inside (radicand) must be $\ge 0$.
Odd roots (cube roots, 5th roots) are fine with negative numbers (e.g., $\sqrt[3]{-8} = -2$).

visual_aids.title: Squaring a Binomial Warning
visual_aids.caption: For the worked example, first note the domain restriction x ≥ 1, then square both sides and expand the binomial.
visual_aids.alt_text: Visual showing the worked equation square root of x plus 5 equals x minus 1. It states that the right side must be non-negative, so x is at least 1, then shows x plus 5 equals (x minus 1) squared and expands to x squared minus 2x plus 1.
visual_aids.data: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 500 230"><rect width="500" height="230" rx="10" fill="#f8fafc"/><text x="250" y="34" font-family="monospace" font-size="20" text-anchor="middle" fill="#0f172a" font-weight="bold">√(x + 5) = x − 1</text><rect x="70" y="48" width="360" height="34" rx="6" fill="#dcfce7" stroke="#16a34a"/><text x="250" y="70" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" fill="#166534" font-weight="bold">Domain check: x − 1 ≥ 0, so x ≥ 1</text><path d="M250 86 L250 105" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2"/><text x="290" y="100" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#1d4ed8">Now square both sides</text><text x="250" y="132" font-family="monospace" font-size="19" text-anchor="middle" fill="#0f172a" font-weight="bold">x + 5 = (x − 1)²</text><rect x="70" y="150" width="360" height="62" rx="6" fill="#fee2e2" stroke="#ef4444" stroke-width="2"/><text x="250" y="173" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" fill="#b91c1c" font-weight="bold">Expand the entire binomial</text><text x="250" y="197" font-family="monospace" font-size="17" text-anchor="middle" fill="#991b1b" font-weight="bold">x + 5 = x² − 2x + 1</text></svg>

solution_steps: Step 1: Since the square root is non-negative, the right-hand side must also be non-negative: $x-1\ge0$, so first state the domain restriction $x\ge1$. Now square both sides: $x+5=(x-1)^2$.
Step 2: FOIL the right side: $x + 5 = x^2 - 2x + 1$.
Step 3: Move everything to one side to form a quadratic: $0 = x^2 - 3x - 4$.

common_mistakes.mistake: Squaring individual terms.
common_mistakes.correction: If you have $\sqrt{x} + 2 = 5$, squaring both sides means $(\sqrt{x} + 2)^2 = 5^2$. It does NOT mean $x + 4 = 25$. This is why you must ALWAYS isolate the radical first, so you are just squaring $(\sqrt{x})^2 = 3^2$.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming all calculated roots are valid.
common_mistakes.correction: Radical equations are notorious for generating fake (extraneous) solutions. Checking your answers by plugging them back into the original prompt is a mandatory step, not an optional one.

quick_summary: Isolate the radical on one side of the equals sign.
Raise both sides to the power of the index (square for square roots, cube for cube roots).
Solve the resulting equation.
Check all answers in the original equation to weed out extraneous solutions.

hs_math_t04_st17.title: Equations and inequalities involving absolute values
hs_math_t04_st17.overview: Absolute value measures distance on the number line and is never negative. Equations involving absolute values can have two solutions, one solution or no solution, while inequalities describe one or more intervals of values. Use distance and number-line reasoning to solve and represent these solution sets.

key_concepts.definition: Distance from zero or from a specified centre.
details: $|x|$ is the non-negative distance of $x$ from zero.
$|x-a|$ is the distance between $x$ and $a$. For example, $|x-3|=2$ means that $x$ is two units from $3$.

key_concepts.definition: Split into two cases.
details: For $a\ge0$, $|u|=a$ means $u=a$ or $u=-a$.
If the right-hand side is negative, an equation of the form $|u|=a$ has no real solution because absolute value cannot be negative.
Both candidate values must be checked in the original equation.

key_concepts.definition: Translate a distance condition into an interval or two rays.
details: For $a>0$, $|u|<a$ is equivalent to $-a<u<a$, and $|u|\le a$ is equivalent to $-a\le u\le a$.
For $a>0$, $|u|>a$ is equivalent to $u<-a$ or $u>a$; the non-strict form uses $\le$ and $\ge$.
Less-than inequalities describe values within a distance; greater-than inequalities describe values outside that distance.

key_concepts.definition: Show which endpoints belong to the solution.
details: Use a closed endpoint when the boundary is included and an open endpoint when it is excluded.
Use a single interval for values between two boundaries, and a union of two intervals for values outside two boundaries.

formulas.name: Absolute Value Non-Strict Inequalities
formulas.equation: $$|u|\le a\iff -a\le u\le a,\quad |u|\ge a\iff u\le-a\text{ or }u\ge a,\quad a\ge0$$

Step 1: Use the outside-interval rule: $x+2<-4$ or $x+2>4$.
Step 3: Both endpoints are excluded because the inequality is strict.

common_mistakes.mistake: Writing only one solution for $|x-a|=b$ when $b>0$.
common_mistakes.correction: An absolute-value equation usually produces two cases, one on either side of the centre. Solve both unless the cases coincide.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using AND instead of OR for a greater-than absolute-value inequality.
common_mistakes.correction: A value more than a units away lies on either side of the centre, so the result is two separate intervals joined by OR.

common_mistakes.mistake: Including endpoints in a strict inequality.
common_mistakes.correction: For $<$ or $>$, the boundary is excluded. Use open endpoints and parentheses in interval notation.

quick_summary: Absolute value represents non-negative distance.
$|u|=a$ gives two cases when $a>0$ and no solution when $a<0$.
Less-than inequalities describe an interval between boundaries; greater-than inequalities describe two outside intervals.
Use number lines and interval notation to represent the solution set.

hs_math_t04_st15.title: Word problems using equations
hs_math_t04_st15.overview: Mathematics models the real world. Solving word problems is the art of translating English sentences into algebraic equations to find unknown quantities.

key_concepts.definition: Naming the unknown.
details: Before writing any equations, explicitly state what your variable represents (e.g., 'Let $x$ be the child's age').
If there are multiple unknowns, relate them to the first variable (e.g., 'Then the parent's age is $3x$').

key_concepts.definition: English to Math.
details: **Addition:** Sum, increased by, more than.
**Subtraction:** Difference, decreased by, less than. (Note: '5 less than x' is $x - 5$, NOT $5 - x$).
**Multiplication:** Product, twice, times, of (e.g., 'half of x' is $\frac{1}{2}x$).
**Equality:** Is, equals, yields, results in.

key_concepts.definition: Standard setups.
details: **Consecutive Integers:** $x$, $x+1$, $x+2$.
**Consecutive Even/Odd Integers:** $x$, $x+2$, $x+4$.
**Distance/Speed/Time:** Distance = Speed $\times$ Time ($D = ST$).

worked_examples.problem: A parent is three times as old as their child. Their combined age is 48 years. Find their present ages.
solution_steps: Step 1: Define variables. Let $x$ = child's age. Then the parent's age = $3x$.
Step 2: Translate the relationship to an equation. Combined age is 48, so $x + 3x = 48$.
Step 4: Answer the prompt. Child is 12. Parent is $3(12) = 36$.

worked_examples.problem: The product of two consecutive positive integers is 90. Find the integers.
solution_steps: Step 1: Define variables. Let $x$ = first integer. Let $x+1$ = second integer.
Step 3: Expand and set to zero: $x^2 + x - 90 = 0$.
Step 5: Context check. The problem specified POSITIVE integers, so reject $-10$.

common_mistakes.mistake: Translating 'less than' backwards.
common_mistakes.correction: 'Ten less than a number' is translated as $x - 10$. Many students write $10 - x$, which is completely incorrect and will ruin the equation.

common_mistakes.mistake: Accepting mathematically valid but physically impossible answers.
common_mistakes.correction: If your quadratic equation says a rectangle's width is $-5$ meters, you must reject it. Always interpret the math back into the real-world context.

quick_summary: Explicitly define your variables first.
Translate English keywords into math operations.
Solve the equation.
Check if the answer makes sense in the real world (no negative ages or distances).

hs_math_t04_st16.title: Systems of equations and applications
hs_math_t04_st16.overview: Some real-world problems contain two unknown quantities connected by two different conditions. A system of simultaneous equations models both conditions together, allowing the unknown quantities to be determined consistently. This lesson focuses on constructing and interpreting the model; the algebraic solution methods are covered earlier.

key_concepts.definition: Choose variables that represent the quantities in context.
details: Define each variable clearly, including its unit where relevant.
Use the wording of the problem to identify the conditions that connect the unknowns.

key_concepts.definition: Translate each independent condition into an equation.
details: A total-count condition may produce an equation such as $x+y=35$.
A cost or revenue condition may produce another equation, such as $12x+8y=340$.
Each equation represents a separate condition, and both must be satisfied by the same values.

key_concepts.definition: Return to the real-world meaning.
details: Solve the system using substitution or elimination from the previous lesson.
Check the values in both original conditions, confirm units and consider any context restrictions such as whole-number counts or non-negative quantities.
State the answer in words, not only as an ordered pair.

variables.x, y: Unknown quantities defined by the problem
variables.a_i, b_i, c_i: Constants obtained from the two conditions

worked_examples.problem: A school event sells 35 tickets. Adult tickets cost 12 units each and student tickets cost 8 units each. Total revenue is 340 units. How many of each ticket were sold?
solution_steps: Step 1: Let $a$ be the number of adult tickets and $s$ be the number of student tickets.
Step 4: From the first equation, $s=35-a$. Substitute: $12a+8(35-a)=340$.

worked_examples.problem: A stationery order contains 40 items made up of notebooks and pens. Each notebook costs 3 units and each pen costs 2 units. The total cost is 95 units. Find the number of each item.
solution_steps: Step 1: Let $n$ be the number of notebooks and $p$ the number of pens.
Step 4: From $p=40-n$, substitute into the cost equation: $3n+2(40-n)=95$.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using only one condition to build a model.
common_mistakes.correction: A system needs one equation for each independent condition in the problem. Define the variables first, then translate every relevant condition.

common_mistakes.mistake: Giving an answer that does not make sense in context.
common_mistakes.correction: Ticket counts and item counts must be whole numbers and cannot be negative. Check the solution against the original wording and units.

quick_summary: Define the unknown quantities clearly.
Translate each independent condition into an equation.
Solve the simultaneous system using a method from ST05.
Check both equations and interpret the answer in context.
